video_title: From Chicago Pit Trader to Robinhood Exec · Steve Quirk
gist: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood and a Chicago options market maker since 1987, walks from the pit through thinkorswim and TD Ameritrade to Robinhood, arguing that the retail playing field has been leveled in ways nobody in the late '80s could have imagined. The substance for investors sits in the operating disclosures (27.5 million Robinhood customers, half new to the market, average age 36, ~98% of options trades on mobile, IPO allocations rising from 1-2% to 20%, average PDT-flagged account of $13,000) and in his structural theses: retail participation growth is a secular acceleration rather than a COVID blip, international retail penetration in the teens is the next leg of growth, and access barriers like PDT and accreditation rules are falling.

insights.claim: Steve Quirk argues the defining psychological edge of professional trading is accepting a ~50% wrong rate as normal, with 51% correct being sufficient to win, a wiring almost no other business tolerates.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A base-rate framing worth importing to portfolio review: judge process and expectancy rather than hit rate, and size positions so a 50% loss rate is survivable.
insights.quote: there's an expectation that you're going to be wrong about 50% of the time and you're good with it

insights.claim: Quirk's market-making risk routine was to price the absolute worst-case outcome of a trade first and then work upward to the best case, so that the downside scenario, if it arrives, triggers no emotional reaction.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A pre-mortem discipline that converts drawdowns from surprises into priced-in events; the practical test of any position is whether you have written down its worst case before entering.
insights.quote: we look at the absolute worst case scenario of that trade and then work our way up to what's the best case scenario

insights.claim: Quirk attributes panic selling primarily to investors never having quantified their maximum downside, and secondarily to position sizes that are simply too large.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Two diagnosable failure modes: if a client or a strategy cannot state its max loss, forced liquidation risk is understated regardless of the thesis quality.
insights.quote: The people that panicked the most with investments or trades are the ones that don't understand what the what the largest downside is because when when it hits they they just freak out.

insights.claim: Quirk identifies myopic fixation on a single losing trade as the fastest way traders fail, arguing that the ability to abandon a position and move on is a prerequisite for survival because not every trade can be repaired.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Screen strategies and traders for the willingness to take a loss and reset; inability to detach is a leading indicator of blow-up risk.
insights.quote: You can't In other words, you can't always fix something. You got to just flick it and move on.

insights.claim: Quirk says holding an uncomfortable position is the worst place to be in investing because discomfort itself produces bad decisions, and he recommends moving whatever percentage restores comfort into cash sweep rather than white-knuckling volatility.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Reframes de-risking as decision hygiene rather than market timing; a practical rule for advisors managing client behavior in drawdowns.
insights.quote: the worst place you can be in the world of investing is in an uncomfortable position because you're going to make a bad decision

insights.claim: During quiet periods on the trading floor, Quirk and colleagues would deliberately force trades to see whether they could work around them into profitability, a habit distinct from the discipline of cutting losers.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A candid admission that even professionals manufacture activity in dead tape; a behavior to monitor and cost out in any discretionary trading operation.

insights.claim: Across the 1987 crash, dot-com, the financial crisis, COVID and the meme era, Quirk's common thread is that crises are triggered by previously unknown mechanisms rather than the risks everyone is already fearful of, citing credit default swaps before 2007-08 as the example.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Argues that consensus tail-risk hedges are usually mispriced against the wrong catalyst; the useful work is inventorying instruments and plumbing nobody has stress-tested.
insights.quote: it's not the known that causes these, it's the unknown

insights.claim: Before October 1987 there was effectively no options skew, with a 10% out-of-the-money put and a 10% out-of-the-money call priced evenly, a convention the crash permanently destroyed.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Concrete reminder that persistent put skew is a learned artifact of one event, not a law of nature, and that regime shifts can reprice option surfaces permanently.
insights.quote: the market, you know, walks up the steps and falls out the window

insights.claim: After the 1987 crash, exchanges shortened trading hours to roughly 9:30 to 1:30 because there was no clarity on which clearing firms and trading firms would even survive, and circuit-breaker halts did not yet exist.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for session-shortening as a crisis tool; counterparty and clearing solvency, not price, was the binding constraint.

insights.claim: Quirk credits the 2010 flash crash with producing the limit up / limit down bands and triggers that now govern US equity markets, arguing that market structure reliably improves after each unforeseen dislocation.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Supports a structurally constructive read on post-crisis regulation: each event narrows the specific failure mode, pushing the next crisis into a new channel.

insights.claim: Quirk says the open-outcry pits ran on an enforced code of honor where a trader's word was binding on disputed 'out trades', and anyone who would not honor the protocol was quickly frozen out of trading.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: The reputational settlement layer of the pits was replaced by clearing and matching technology; a lens for evaluating trust assumptions in newer venues.
insights.quote: your your word is your bond

insights.claim: Quirk's floor-trading firm paid roughly $10,000 a month for a brick-sized handheld delivering quotes and order entry, functionality he says is now inferior to what any retail user gets free on an iPhone.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark for how completely the market-data and execution moat has eroded; the surviving edge in brokerage is distribution and design, not tooling.
insights.quote: it cost us 10 grand a month. 10 grand a month we paid for that technology

insights.claim: In the late 1980s retail investors paid $75 to $80 per trade while floor professionals paid essentially nothing, and also lacked the information access and education professionals had, a three-part gap Quirk says has now been closed.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Quantifies the commission compression that underwrote the retail participation boom; the remaining differentials are product access, not price.

insights.claim: European exchange demutualization opened market making to anyone and drove the build-out of broad electronic access technology roughly seven or eight years before the equivalent shift reached the US.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A template for how ownership structure gates technology adoption; watch mutualized or member-owned venues elsewhere as candidates for the same repricing of access.
insights.quote: as soon as they went public, now the whole world is a market maker. Anybody can be a market maker.

insights.claim: Quirk points to Interactive Brokers as the firm that converted a floor market-making technology edge into a retail brokerage business, having built tools on the trading floor that competitors lacked and operating globally across exchanges.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for the market-maker-to-broker path that shaped IBKR's structural cost advantage in retail.

insights.claim: Quirk recounts that TD Ameritrade's marketing team proposed renaming thinkorswim 'the ultimate trading platform' after the 2009 acquisition, and Tom Sosnoff defeated it by commissioning his own brand-recognition survey after dismissing theirs.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Illustrates how acquirer-side brand instincts can destroy the exact community equity that justified the deal price, relevant to any fintech acquisition thesis.

insights.claim: Robinhood has roughly 27.5 million customers of whom about half are new to the market, and Quirk frames financial literacy delivery as a suitability obligation created by that mix.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Half the base being first-time investors is both the growth story and the regulatory exposure; education spend should be modeled as a compliance cost, not marketing.
insights.quote: half of our 27 and a half million customers are new to the market

insights.claim: Quirk says Robinhood is the largest retail options trading firm and until recently executed about 98% of its options trades on a phone, a share now closer to 95% as the desktop Legend platform grows.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Mobile-native options flow at this scale is a distinctive order-flow profile; the Legend-driven shift toward desktop signals a deliberate move upmarket into more active traders.
insights.quote: the largest option retail option trading firm, which is Robinhood today, is doing 98% of their trades on a phone

insights.claim: Robinhood reaches roughly 60% of US households and about 10% of the US adult population holds an account, figures the firm uses in conversations with regulators and elected officials.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Household penetration at that level makes domestic account growth a saturation story and reframes the growth case around international expansion and wallet share.

insights.claim: Quirk pushes back on the perception that Robinhood is dominated by all-day active traders, saying the lion's share of customers are buy-and-hold investors who allocate only a small slice of the portfolio to whatever theme is hot, such as AI or energy story stocks.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: If accurate, Robinhood's revenue is less cyclical than a pure day-trading proxy implies, and its flow is a barometer of retail thematic allocation rather than churn.
insights.quote: Most of them, you know, are people that are buy and hold.

insights.claim: Robinhood's average customer age is 36 versus roughly 60 at TD Ameritrade and Schwab, which Quirk says forces a different education model: contextual, on-demand learning inside the product pathway rather than long-form in-person seminars.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A 24-year age gap between platforms implies decades of asset-transfer tailwind for the younger franchise and different product economics at each.
insights.quote: average age is 60, and they they learn in a different way than, you know, the people that are in their 30s

insights.claim: Quirk cites Robinhood cash sweep paying around 3 to 3.5%, which he tells nervous investors is roughly 20 times a bank deposit rate, positioning it as the release valve for volatility discomfort.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Cash sweep is doubling as a retention product that keeps de-risking clients on-platform rather than transferring to banks, a meaningful net-interest and stickiness lever.
insights.quote: That is 20 times what you're getting at your bank.

insights.claim: Quirk argues the retail participation surge during the stimulus-check and meme-stock era was an acceleration of a long-running secular trend rather than a blip, noting retail's share has continued rising across equities, options, crypto and futures.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: The core structural bet behind retail brokerage valuations; if the trend is secular, drawdowns in retail volumes are cyclical entry points rather than trend breaks.
insights.quote: I just thought it was an acceleration of what was already happening

insights.claim: Quirk says the pattern day trader rule is going away as of this episode's airing, after a multi-year push by brokerage firms, exchanges and other market participants that began before his time at Robinhood.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Removal of the $25,000 equity constraint expands the addressable active-trading base at every retail broker and should show up first in small-account turnover.

insights.claim: The average Robinhood account affected by PDT is about $13,000, meaning the rule disproportionately constrained the platform's youngest and smallest customers.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Sizes the affected cohort directly: PDT repeal is a volume unlock concentrated in small accounts, the segment most likely to trade options and leveraged products.

insights.claim: Quirk argues PDT was a reasonable dot-com-era rule that became obsolete once clearing-firm and broker risk systems caught up 10 to 15 years ago, and that its main effects since have been forcing traders to hold losers to avoid flags and driving them to transfer accounts to another broker after being flagged.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Names PDT-driven account churn as a real customer-acquisition cost across retail brokers; repeal should improve retention economics industry-wide.
insights.quote: as soon as they hit their flag, they just transfer out of Robinhood and go open an account at the broker XYZ and start over

insights.claim: Quirk says he used to teach traders to move into futures specifically to escape PDT, preferring the ES future over SPY because futures carry no day-trade count and no short-sale restrictions.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Part of retail futures volume was regulatory arbitrage rather than product preference, so PDT repeal could pull some of that flow back into cash equities and ETFs.
insights.quote: Trade futures. They don't have these stupid rules.

insights.claim: Robinhood's IPO Access allocations have shifted from the firm scratching and clawing for 1% to 2% of a deal to issuers proactively offering 20%, which Quirk calls the most positive development for retail customers.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A tenfold shift in retail allocation power changes IPO book-building dynamics and gives retail platforms a genuine issuer-side product to monetize.
insights.quote: we used to scratch and claw to get 1% or 2%. Now, we're having firms come to us and say we want to give you 20%.

insights.claim: Quirk attacks accreditation rules as illogical, contrasting a 54-year-old who inherited a $10 million windfall being deemed qualified against a 31-year-old NASA space engineer who is not, and signals more access barriers are targeted next.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Flags the accredited-investor definition as the next regulatory wall the retail platforms will push on, with private-market and pre-IPO access as the prize.
insights.quote: suddenly I'm more qualified to to to make an investment uh than a 31-year-old NASA space engineer? I don't think so

insights.claim: Quirk lists retail demand for around-the-clock trading, pre-IPO securities and institutional-style IPO allocation as the specific asks driving Robinhood's product roadmap, framed as customers pushing the firm once existing capabilities are delivered.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A stated roadmap of the next products to expect from retail brokers; each is a potential fee pool and a competitive gap for incumbents that lack them.

insights.claim: Retail investing participation is in the teens as a share in both Europe and Asia versus roughly 60% of US households, which Quirk identifies as the core headroom behind Robinhood's decision to expand abroad.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Quantifies the international TAM gap that underpins the growth case now that US household penetration is high.
insights.quote: as great as the retail participation is in the US, 60% of US households, it's in the teens in Europe, it's in the teens in Asia

insights.claim: Quirk estimates 75 to 80% of what international customers want is US equities that Robinhood already offers, with the remaining local work being country-specific wrappers such as UK ISAs and SIPPs plus FX conversion.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Implies unusually low marginal cost to international launches, since the product core ships unchanged and only tax wrappers and FX need localization.

insights.claim: Quirk says regulators and elected officials abroad welcome retail brokerage entrants because household investment wealth reduces citizens' reliance on the government at retirement, producing warm receptions in initial country conversations.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Pension-burden politics is an underappreciated tailwind for cross-border retail brokerage licensing, lowering perceived regulatory entry risk.

insights.claim: Quirk describes Asian and particularly Chinese investors as operating a 'barbell economy' mindset, risking a larger share of assets in markets than US or European investors because rapid wage growth backstops them, while financial literacy there lags the US.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Higher risk budgets plus lower literacy means Asian retail expansion carries both higher revenue per account and higher suitability and conduct risk.
insights.quote: They're they're more prone to take risk.

insights.claim: Quirk frames self-directed investing as delivering personal agency for a generation expected to hold four or five jobs by age 30, enabling career breaks funded by investment income rather than employment.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: The narrative retail brokers will use with regulators and younger customers alike; it reframes trading access as labor-market flexibility rather than speculation.

insights.claim: Quirk cites today's sub-16 to 18 VIX despite the list of negative catalysts as the market lesson that recently changed his thinking, concluding you never fully figure markets out and must keep learning.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A practitioner flagging compressed volatility as inconsistent with the macro backdrop, the setup where cheap convexity is worth revisiting.
insights.quote: I've learned to never say never.
